sections.history: Kumbakonam is among the most temple-dense of Tamil towns, clustered around the sacred Mahamaham tank. The Kasi Viswanathar temple here is held by many devotees — and by its own priests — to be the Kudanthai Karonam praised in the Tevaram, the shrine the saints Appar and Sambandar sang. The claim is shared: priests of the nearby Someswarar temple maintain that theirs is the Tevaram Karonam, and both traditions have long coexisted. The stone temple carries Chola work with substantial Nayak-period expansion.
sections.architecture: The temple is a Dravidian complex whose tallest tower is the western gopuram, rising seven storeys to about 72 feet. Within, the sanctum enshrines the lingam worshipped as Kaaroneswarar. Its setting beside the Mahamaham tank places it at the heart of Kumbakonam's sacred geography, among the ring of temples that draw pilgrims to the town's famous twelve-yearly Mahamaham festival.
sections.legends: The name Kayarohaneswarar is explained by the tradition of a devotee embracing the lingam — kaya, the body, arohana, ascent or clasping — the name later shortening to Karonam. Another tradition links the name to Rama, who is said to have absorbed the essence of Rudra here. As with much of Kumbakonam's sacred lore, these stories belong to the dense web of legend that gathers around the Mahamaham tank, into which, it is believed, the waters of the sacred rivers descend.
sections.festivals: The temple shares in Kumbakonam's great festival life, above all the Mahamaham, held once in twelve years, when pilgrims in their lakhs bathe in the tank and the town's temples open their processions. The Shaiva calendar — Maha Shivaratri, Pradosham and the Margazhi season — is kept with the vigour of a major temple town, and the tall western gopuram presides over it all.
sections.experience: To visit the Karonam at Kumbakonam is to step into one of the densest concentrations of sanctity in the Tamil land. Pilgrims move among the town's many shrines and the Mahamaham tank, and the darshan of Kaaroneswarar is part of a larger pilgrimage through a sacred townscape layered with Chola stone and living tradition.

visit.timings: Typically open from early morning to midday and again from late afternoon into the evening; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected, with shoulders and knees covered; footwear is left at the entrance.
visit.photography: Photography is generally allowed in the outer corridors but not inside the sanctum; ask temple staff before photographing rituals.
visit.gettingThere: The temple is in Kumbakonam town, Thanjavur district, near the Mahamaham tank; Kumbakonam has its own railway station and is well connected by bus from Thanjavur, Mayiladuthurai and Chennai.
